t: Strategies to help students experience success
q: As a teacher, however, I have come to focus on the second part more and I think that is our job in a nutshell. We are changing the things that we can through instructing, modelling and supporting our students, continually adapting to our classes.

Why: Students will struggle to achieve any success if they don’t have the material to access when answering questions about a topic. We cannot expect them to simply guess what we have in our heads, especially if they have missed a lesson for any reason.

Ebbinghaus’ forgetting curve is famous as it gives us a template of forgetting that we can work with when teaching and encouraging retrieval. When students first learn something, the retention rate is very high but over time, this drops.

My previous style of teaching would include teaching them a concept followed by a worksheet with questions where they applied their new learning. I always had some students in every class who simply could not access the questions and if they did attempt them, would use keywords incorrectly or miss out important detail. I would go and support them but this is a reactive response to something that I could have avoided from the start.

This is something I resisted for a very long time despite reading about its benefits in the classroom. I was worried my older GCSE students would laugh at the thought of doing it. Nonetheless, I trialled it with my classes and found it oddly reassuring.

The biggest hurdle is a lack of prerequisite knowledge but sometimes this could be all we focus on and students miss out on actually writing well reasoned and detailed responses. The best way to get students to achieve good writing is by getting them to practice good writing.

Ultimately, we want to develop confident learners so they can attempt challenging questions and make important connections between concepts. But the first step? Provide students with chances to experience small successes so they can move on to bigger ones.

t: Why Is This So Hard? On Workload, Pressure, and the Ways through the Woods
q: I expected the year to be different — but I didn't expect to be drowning in a way that I haven't felt since my first years.
I began asking more people how they were doing. I was surprised at how few were doing well.
But the workload this year is especially hard because the added task volume is A) not skippable, B) very difficult, or C) too new to know how important it is.
Pressure makes our minds mushy. It makes giving in to distraction easier. It goads us into using brute force — working harder — to solve problems that require tactical savvy.
I'll say it: we may need to sacrifice or severely modify our pedagogy this year. I'm starting to accept this.
Times like this call for deeper, longer draws from the springs of well-being — not shallower, quicker ones.

We've got to approach this like learners. When someone you are with shares something that helps them in the physical or mental or emotional or spiritual or social elements of their lives, get out the notebook. Write it down.

t: Two Simple Techniques for Increasing Meaningful Interaction During In-Person PD
q: At the keynote, Darlene heard from leadership developer Lowell Applebaum, whose session emphasized a dispositional skillset we'd like all of our students and colleagues to have: listening to understand v. listening to reply.

We all had name tags, but to increase our getting to know each other, he had us all put a sticky note below our names that read "Ask me about…" I filled in "Retirement." Then we were off meeting others with what they had written as opposed to just their names.

The speaker also had us… take out our cell phones and find a picture that we could talk about. Then the same routine. I used a photo I had taken last week of a bull moose and a cow standing in the river that runs behind my house.
This was fun and a great way to learn something about someone besides just their name and title; it created a stronger interest and memory.

My principals at Cedar Springs High School have done something like this to kick off our staff meetings. It certainly is an enjoyable way to break the ice or build connection at the start of a meeting.
x: Both techniques target a specific disposition — listening to understand rather than listening to reply — that a facilitator can deliberately design into the structure of a session's icebreaker.

Both techniques are designed to shift participants from 'listening to reply' toward 'listening to understand,' a disposition Stuart argues produces more meaningful conversations and more constructive debate among adults.
The second, 'Pick a Picture,' has participants share and discuss a photo from their own phone, which Stuart notes his own principals have used to open staff meetings.
'Pick a Picture' uses a photo already on a participant's phone as a low-prep conversation starter that builds interest and memory more effectively than generic icebreaker prompts.

q: Ensuring our students know, understand and remember the facts is vital. This is the foundation on which we can build connections between topics and ideas. In fact, it is only once this foundation is developed and secure that our students can truly apply what they know to new contexts and recognise patterns.
Personally, I don’t believe this is the case at all. I think we can all accept that knowledge does indeed give us power. However, I would also add that knowing stuff is joyous.
When a passionate Science teacher reads a fascinating Science news story, do they need a video to go with it to feel engaged? Do they need the story in the form of a game to maintain their interest?

When you teach a novice learner, which most (if not all) secondary students are, you try and impart all the knowledge they need in your subject to make sense of the world. Using drill allows this to happen without distractions, without overloading their working memories and with the focus purely on learning.
People feel euphoric when something clicks and they finally get something. Think back to when this happened in your class. Pure joy all around!

So how do we help our students experience this joy of obtaining knowledge? The obvious thing to do is to teach really well, without gimmicks, embed consistent routines and get our students to continually retrieve information so application becomes easier with time.
x: For novices, drill removes distraction and protects working memory so that facts become secure, after which students can apply and appreciate them.
Castelino argues that knowing things is itself joyous, so knowledge-rich teaching need not cost students wonder.

Her claim is that secure prior knowledge is the precondition of joy, since a passionate expert enjoys a news story because she has the schemas to connect and evaluate it, not because it arrives as a video or game.
Drill is defended as a way to impart knowledge to novices without overloading working memory.
The moment of understanding something that finally clicks is presented as the real source of classroom joy.
Her recommended practice is gimmick-free teaching, consistent routines, continual retrieval and storytelling from the discipline.

t: Weekends Can Restore, But They Don't Do It On Autopilot: Here Are Two Simple Practices That Can Help ple-practices-that-can-help
q: Which of the things or people I say "Yes" to and which of the things or people I say "No" to is of critical import — my very life, and the lives of those to whom I most owe my love, will be determined by the sum of my yes or no decisions.

I'm starting to learn that weekend is a verb and an art and a craft. Weekending well — in a way that restores me and my family for the week to come — takes practice, intentionality, study, and inquiry.

Find a trail or a park or a backyard near where you live, and go there to sit or walk for twenty minutes. No earbuds, no phones. Your goal is to be quiet amidst other things that are A) alive and B) unable to make demands on you.

The idea is simple: for 24 hours straight, you don't read or think or write or check email about work. You don't do paper stacks, you don't do mindless grading while watching a movie — work just doesn't exist for those 24 hours.
For go-getters like Crystal and me, what we're most challenged and restored by in the 24 hours is the idea that the world doesn't depend on our performance or our keeping up with things.

Regardless of your philosophical bent, may I strongly recommend the 24-Hour Challenge to you, too. It is such a good practice for those of us educators who want to maximize the long-term flourishing outcomes of our classrooms while not sacrificing our lives on the altar of professional success.
x: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that weekends don't automatically restore a person the way many teachers assume — 'weekending well' is a practiced art and craft requiring the same intentionality that structures the workweek.

t: Inside the Mind of a Master Teacher: Here's How Lynsay Fabio Would Approach Classroom Management During Distance Learning oach-classroom-management-during-distance-learning
q: Classroom management is about protecting every child's right to learn and enjoy amazing academic experiences.
I am the right person for this job. There is no one with a cape flying in after me. I'm the best we've got right now. I am not perfect, but I am enough.
It's way easier to allow more freedom once I've got the tone I want than to suddenly start taking away freedoms that once existed.
Students are not oblivious — they can tell when their teacher is trying to protect the learning environment rather than just exercising mindless control.

My most basic responsibility as a teacher is to check for their understanding of the lesson as it's happening, and without video, I can't do this — all "hold up your answers" and all hand gestures can't happen without video.
Never mistake good classroom management for the meal itself. But without it, your delicious lesson is going to go to waste.

t: Here's How and Why to Use Guided Meditation as a Teacher During COVID 2020
q: For over twenty years, I've begun my classes with stillness — first as a crowd-control trick; later, because it's the best skill I know to share with kids.
My former students, years after they've graduated, still contact me to say they heard "Orange Sky," one of the calming songs I use in my class, or thank me for introducing them to meditation.
More than any other year, I have needed meditation to get me through these tough times, and that is why I commissioned a special meditation to speak to our struggle.

I called Jess last week and spoke to the fears teachers have about returning to the classroom and how that anxiety and uncertainty can be paralyzing. Jess got it. But what's more, she found a way to bring that fear — that contracting of heart and mind — under control, expanding it into something beautiful.
Some of you might pause at the word hypnotherapy or hypnosis, assuming it means brainwashing someone into doing silly or harmful things. It's not.
Research has found hypnosis can even alter a person's immune function in ways that offset stress and reduce susceptibility to viral infections.

t: A Simple Tweak for Tracking Moments of Genuine Connection in Band
q: I wanted to run with your concept of "Moments of Genuine Connection" tracking sheet but in context for band. At the beginning of the year I was cutting out student photos and scanning them to create a seating chart. It took forever but was worth it to put students' faces and names together.

After printing the chart I put it into a clear sheet in my attendance binder that stays on my conductors music stand. I'm going to take roll with a red dry erase marker and erase it each day when it goes in the computer. I'll be using Blue and Green to mark which students have had certain opportunities in class.

Blue dots will be students with whom I've had a Moment of Genuine Connection. Green dots will be students who have had an opportunity to conduct the band either in warm-ups or a song (public speaking).
As he practices moments of genuine connection with every student on his roster, he'll get better and he'll start to see the profound effects of "the dumbest intervention ever.

He'll begin to detect where his connection blindspots are — who are the students that he has the easiest time missing, week after week? Why? These questions will deepen him in his understanding of himself.

He'll create a classroom where public speaking — in this case, conducting the band — is normal rather than weird. This normalization of what for many students is the scariest thing about school will make Clint's classroom an even more special place in the memories of his students.
Clint is going to succeed because he thought up this strategy while listening to a guy who's only ever taught 6-12 grade English language arts and history.
